p: I'm Kuzey Aydın, I'm eleven, and I'm a Windborn. The winds of the world talk to me, and when I ask nicely, they help.

My grandmother, Nermin, is the Keeper of an old secret society called the Order of the Compass Rose. For nine hundred years, the Order has hidden seven bronze Keys around the world. Each one holds the heart of a great wind. Bring all seven to the Gate of Seven Winds, and you can rule the weather of the whole world.

Mordecai Vane wants to do exactly that. He has a hand of cold gray stone, an army of fog-eyed men called the Grays, and twin children, Vex and Vera. He kidnapped Grandma to make me find the Keys for him.
So far, my cousin Ela, my best friend Bora, Uncle Tarık and I have found three Keys.
The Yıldız, the North Wind, in Istanbul. It lives inside me.
The Lodos, the warm southwest wind, under the palace of Knossos on Crete. Vex took it from me by freezing Uncle Tarık.

The Karayel, the Black Wind, in an ice cave under a glacier in Iceland, guarded by twelve trolls. They're stone now. The Black Wind lives inside me too, next to the North Wind. I promised it that one day, all the winds will be free.
Bora found out he's a Beastspeaker. He can understand animals. A raven called Krummi gave him a feather.
And Vera Vane helped us again. She saved us from the trolls. She says she'll keep helping when she can.
The score is two to one.
Now the next star on the map is glowing in the desert. In the land of the pharaohs.
**Kuzey Aydın,** 11. A Windborn with two winds inside him. When he breathes out, sometimes it snows and sometimes a tiny black cloud comes out.
**Ela Aydın,** 12. Kuzey's cousin. The Clue Book now has fifty-one pages of notes, a newspaper article about a Minotaur, and a pressed Icelandic flower.
**Bora Kaya,** 11. Kuzey's best friend. Beastspeaker. Keeps a raven's feather in his hat.
**Uncle Tarık.** Ela's dad, an archaeologist. Has always, always wanted to go to Egypt.
**Dr. Amira Hassan.** An old friend of Uncle Tarık's. An Egyptologist in Cairo. Laughs very loudly.
**Grandma Nermin.** The Keeper. Prisoner in the gray tower.
**Mordecai Vane.** The Gray Hand. Has one Key. Wants seven.
**Vex Vane,** 13. His son. His fingertips are turning to stone. He hasn't told anyone.
**Vera Vane,** 13. His daughter. She is starting to wonder about her mother's bracelet.
From Iceland to Egypt is a jump from minus ten degrees to plus thirty. My body didn't know what was happening.

I stepped out of Cairo airport into a wall of heat. Hot, dry, dusty heat, like opening an oven. The North Wind and the Black Wind both panicked inside me. The North Wind wanted to freeze everything. The Black Wind wanted to make a storm. They argued about it so loudly in my head that I didn't notice the sneeze coming.
"A-a-a-CHOO!"
I sneezed a tiny snowstorm onto a taxi driver.
It wasn't a big one. Just a little cloud of snowflakes, glittering in the sunshine, swirling around his head and settling on his mustache and his eyebrows and the top of his taxi.
"Sorry!" I said. "Allergies!"

He looked at the snowflakes melting on his mustache. He looked at the blue Egyptian sky, with not a single cloud in it. He looked at me. Then he said something in Arabic that sounded like a prayer, put our bags in his taxi very quickly, and drove us very fast to our hotel without saying another word.
"Allergies?" said Ela, in the back seat. "*Allergies?*"
"It's what Bora's mom says whenever he sneezes on someone."
"Bora's mom," said Bora, "is a very wise woman."

Cairo is the biggest city I have ever seen. Bigger than Istanbul, which I didn't think was possible. Twenty million people. A million car horns, all honking at the same time, all day and all night. Donkey carts next to brand-new cars. Men on bicycles carrying huge trays of bread on their heads, steering through the traffic with one hand. Buildings in every color of sand, from pale yellow to dark brown, stretching away to the horizon, with thousands of minarets rising above them.
And the Nile flowing through the middle of it all, wide and brown and slow, with little white sailboats drifting on it.
And at the edge of the city, rising out of the desert like mountains someone built on purpose, the pyramids.

I saw them from the taxi window, as we came over a bridge. Three of them. Huge and golden and perfect, standing at the edge of the city where the houses stopped and the desert began, shimmering in the heat.
Uncle Tarık saw them too. He made a sound like a whimper.

"The Great Pyramid," he said. He had tears in his eyes. Actual tears. "Four thousand five hundred years old. For almost four thousand years, it was the tallest building on Earth. Kids, this is the best day of my life."
"You said that in Athens," said Ela.
"And Iceland," said Bora.
"I have many best days," said Uncle Tarık happily, wiping his eyes.

The desert wind came in through the taxi window, and it was different from every wind I had met so far. Hot and dry, with a voice like rustling paper. Like pages turning in an old book. It didn't argue, like the Greek winds, or rumble, like the Icelandic ones. It *whispered secrets.* Thousands of them, all at the same time, overlapping, hissing, like sand pouring through fingers.

*The sand remembers,* it hissed. *The sand remembers everything. The pharaohs. The builders. The slaves. The kings. The thieves. The silver-haired woman who came forty years ago and hid a wind in the place of riddles.*
"The place of riddles," I repeated. "Grandma was here. Forty years ago. She hid the Keşişleme somewhere with riddles."
"The Keşişleme," said Ela, writing. "The southeast wind. The wind from the deserts."
She looked out of the window, toward the pyramids. In front of them, small from this distance, crouched a shape. A lion, lying down, with its paws stretched out in front of it. And a human head.
"Only one place in Egypt," she said, "is famous for riddles."

chapters.t: Chapter Two: The City of a Thousand Minarets
p: Our hotel was old and tall and a bit falling down, in the middle of the city, with a lift made of iron bars that rattled and groaned and stopped between floors. From the roof, you could see the whole of Cairo, and the Nile, and the pyramids in the distance.
It was so hot on the roof that the North Wind made a little cloud of frost around my head just to cope.
"Okay," said Ela. She had the Clue Book open on her knee. "Point one. We need to find the Sphinx. Point two..."
"Point one," said Uncle Tarık firmly, "is lunch."
So we went to the bazaar.

The Khan el-Khalili is Cairo's great bazaar, and it reminded me so much of the Grand Bazaar in Istanbul that my chest hurt. The same narrow streets, packed with people. The same shopkeepers standing in their doorways, calling out to everyone who passed. "Hello, my friend! Welcome! Where are you from? Turkey? Turkey, my friend! Very good! Come, come, just looking is free!"

But it was different too. Louder. Brighter. More colors. Brass lamps hanging in clusters like bunches of grapes, with holes cut into them in patterns of stars, so that when they were lit, they threw stars across the walls. Piles of spices in red and orange and yellow and brown, shaped into perfect pyramids. Little statues of cats and pharaohs and scarab beetles. Perfume bottles of colored glass. Carpets. Gold. Silver. Hookah pipes. And the smell. Cumin and cardamom and roasting coffee and grilled meat and something sweet, like rosewater.
Bora was in heaven again.

We ate in a tiny restaurant down a side alley, sitting on little wooden stools. Falafel, which in Egypt is green inside and made from beans, and flatbread, and a dip made from eggplant, and little pickled vegetables, and a sweet pastry soaked in syrup. Bora said Egypt had "moved up to number three" on his list of favorite countries, behind Turkey and Greece, but "only because of the börek situation."

After lunch, while Uncle Tarık was arguing happily with a shopkeeper about whether a little statue was really four thousand years old ("It is NOT, my friend, it was made last Tuesday, look, it says Made in China on the bottom"), I went and stood at the end of the alley, where a little breeze came in from the street.
I listened to the desert wind.

There was so much of it. Secrets, secrets, everywhere. About the man who sold lamps, who had a secret girlfriend. About the cat on the roof, who had eaten a whole fish when nobody was looking. About an old stone, buried under a house down the road, with writing on it that nobody had read for three thousand years.
And then, under all of that, something cold.
*Gray,* whispered the desert wind. *Gray ones in the city. Three of them. At the airport. Asking questions. Asking about a boy who sneezes snow.*
"They know we're here," I said, when I went back to the others. "Already."
"Of course they do," said Ela, not looking up. "They always do. It's like they have a radar." She frowned. "How *do* they always know?"
Nobody had an answer to that.

Uncle Tarık had an old friend from university in Cairo. Dr. Amira Hassan, an Egyptologist, which means someone who studies ancient Egypt. She worked at the Egyptian Museum, a huge old pink building in the middle of the city, full of mummies and gold and statues and things that were five thousand years old.
She met us in her office, at the top of a long, dusty staircase, in a room so full of books and papers and boxes and bits of pottery that it made Uncle Tarık's apartment look tidy.

She was small and quick, with a bright green headscarf, glasses on a chain around her neck, and a laugh you could hear three rooms away. When she saw Uncle Tarık, she shrieked and threw her arms around him.
"Tarık! You haven't changed! You still hold your flashlight upside down!"
Uncle Tarık looked at the flashlight in his hand. It was upside down. He turned it around, embarrassed.
"Amira," he said. "It's been twenty years."
"Twenty-two," said Dr. Amira. "I still have the photo. You with the camel. The camel that sat on you."
"It didn't sit on me," said Uncle Tarık. "It *leaned.*"
"It sat on you," Dr. Amira told us, her eyes twinkling. "For twenty minutes. We could not move it. He was very flat afterward."
Then she looked at the three of us. Ela, with the Clue Book. Bora, eating a falafel from his pocket. Me.
"And these are the famous children," she said. "Your message said something about... wind magic?"
Uncle Tarık looked embarrassed. "It's a long story."
"I love long stories," said Dr. Amira. She cleared four chairs by pushing all the papers onto the floor, and sat down, and folded her hands, and looked at us expectantly.
So we told her. All of it.

Grandma and the storm. The Order of the Compass Rose. The Keys and the Gate. Mordecai and the Grays. Tepegöz in the Cistern, and the carpets in the Bazaar, and the Tower of the Winds, and Talos, and the Minotaur. The geysers and the trolls and Krummi.
I was sure she would laugh. Or call a doctor. Or call the police.
Instead, when we finished, she was quiet for a long, long time.
Then she said, "Show me."
I looked at Uncle Tarık. He nodded.
I breathed out. Very gently. The way Ela had taught me on the roof in Athens.

A little cloud of snowflakes floated across Dr. Amira's office, in the hot, dusty air of Cairo. They sparkled in the sunlight from the window. They drifted down, slowly, and landed on her desk, on her papers, on the ancient pottery, and melted.
Dr. Amira watched them fall. Her face didn't change at all.

Then she stood up. She walked to a locked cabinet in the corner of her office. She opened it with a small key that she wore on a chain around her neck, next to her glasses. And she took out something wrapped in an old white cloth.
She unwrapped it on the desk.

It was a clay tablet. About the size of a paperback book, reddish-brown, very old. Its edges were chipped. And its surface was covered with tiny carved pictures, in neat rows. An eye. A bird. A wavy line, like water. A lion. A feather. A little man sitting down.
"Hieroglyphs," whispered Ela.
"A woman gave me this," said Dr. Amira, "forty years ago."
She sat back down, and her eyes went far away, remembering.

"I was a student. Very young. Very serious. I wanted to be the greatest Egyptologist in the world. One day, I was working late in the museum, alone, and a woman came into the room. I don't know how she got in. The museum was locked." She smiled. "She had silver hair, even then. Very short and spiky. And very sharp eyes. And a necklace with a bronze needle on it."
"Grandma," I said.

"She said, 'You are Amira Hassan.' I said yes. She said, 'One day, a boy who talks to the wind will come asking about the Sphinx. Give him this.' And she gave me the tablet, and she walked out, and I never saw her again." Dr. Amira laughed. "I thought she was a little crazy. But I liked her very much. And I kept the tablet. I have kept it for forty years. Every year, on my birthday, I take it out and read it, and I wonder what it means."
She handed it to me.

It was warm. Not warm like something left in the sun. Warm from inside, like a cup of tea. And it smelled of the desert. Of hot sand and spices and something else, something wild and dry and far away.
The Keşişleme. I could feel it. Very faint, like a voice in another room.
Ela leaned over it. "Can you read it?"
"Of course," said Dr. Amira. "I have been reading it every year for forty years, wondering what it meant. I know it by heart."
She traced the little pictures with her finger, one by one, and read it out.

§CLUE The lion with a man's face has asked one riddle for five thousand years. Ask him for his second. Answer it truly, when the sun stands between his paws, and the wind of the southeast will rise from the sand.
"The lion with a man's face," said Bora. "That's the Sphinx. Even I know that."

"The Sphinx's riddle," said Ela slowly. "Everyone knows the Sphinx's riddle. In the Greek story. 'What walks on four legs in the morning, two in the afternoon, and three in the evening?' The answer is a human. But that was a different Sphinx. A Greek one. In Thebes."

"The Greeks borrowed the Sphinx from the Egyptians," said Dr. Amira, "the way they borrowed many things. But ours is the original. And according to some very, very old stories, the ones that are not in any book, our Sphinx has *two* riddles. One that he asks everyone. And one that he only asks if you know to ask for it."
"His second riddle," I said.
"The one nobody has ever answered," said Dr. Amira. "Or so the stories say."

chapters.t: Chapter Five: The Sun Between His Paws
p: "When the sun stands between his paws," I said, reading it again. "Is that a time of day? Like Galata Tower, at sunset?"
Dr. Amira's eyes sparkled.

"Twice a year," she said, "on the equinox, in spring and autumn, when day and night are exactly the same length, something special happens at Giza. If you stand in a certain spot, at sunset, the sun sets exactly between the Sphinx and the pyramid behind him. Like a golden ball, balanced on his back." She smiled. "Or near enough. People come from all over the world to see it."
"So we have to go on the equinox," said Bora. "At sunset. When is it?"
Ela was already looking at her phone. Her face fell.
"The next equinox is in March," she said. "That's *months* away. Three and a half months!"

We all looked at each other. Three and a half months. Grandma in the gray tower for three and a half more months. Mordecai searching for the other Keys for three and a half months. And the Grays, already in Cairo, asking about a boy who sneezes snow.
"We can't wait that long," I said. "We can't."
"Ah," said Dr. Amira. She took off her glasses and cleaned them on her headscarf, smiling a little smile. "But I said the *sun.* I did not say the sun in the sky."
We stared at her.
"What does that mean?" said Bora.

"It means," said Dr. Amira, putting her glasses back on, "that I have an idea. A very good idea. And a little bit crazy." She stood up. "Come with me. I want to show you something in the museum. And on the way, I will tell you about Shu."
"Who's Shu?" said Bora.
"The god of the wind," said Dr. Amira.

chapters.t: Chapter Six: The God Who Held Up the Sky
p: The Egyptian Museum is like a giant attic. A giant attic belonging to a family of pharaohs who never threw anything away for five thousand years.

There are statues everywhere. Huge ones, ten meters tall, of kings sitting on thrones with their hands on their knees. Little ones, of cats and hawks and crocodiles and baboons. Statues of scribes, sitting cross-legged with papyrus on their laps. Statues of queens, smiling secret smiles. There are coffins painted gold and blue, shaped like people, with big painted eyes. There are wooden boats, and chariots, and beds, and chairs, and sandals, and jars of food that are four thousand years old.
And there are mummies.
Dr. Amira took us through room after room, talking the whole time, walking very fast. Bora kept stopping to stare at things. Uncle Tarık kept stopping to stare at things and make little happy noises.

"Shu," said Dr. Amira, "was the god of the air. Of the wind. Of the empty space between the earth and the sky. In our old stories, the earth was a god called Geb, lying down, and the sky was a goddess called Nut, arching over him, covered in stars. And Shu stood between them, holding up the sky with his arms, so that it would not fall down on the earth. So there would be space for people to live. To breathe."

She stopped in front of a painting on the side of a coffin. It showed a man standing with his arms raised, holding up a woman whose body was stretched out above him like a bridge, covered in tiny painted stars. Under his feet lay another man, green, with plants growing out of him.

"Shu holds up the sky," said Dr. Amira softly. "The wind holds up the sky. Without the wind, the Egyptians believed, there would be no air. No breath. No life. The wind is not just a storm. The wind is the breath of the world."
I looked at the painting for a long time. The man with his arms up. Holding up the whole sky.
*He was a good one,* whispered the desert wind, very softly, through a crack in the museum window. *Shu. The Egyptians understood us. They did not try to own us. They thanked us.*

Dr. Amira led us down a staircase, into the basement. Along a long corridor, past doors marked STORAGE and NO ENTRY and DANGER: DO NOT ENTER, in Arabic and English. She unlocked a door with a key from her chain and switched on a light.

The room was full of shelves, and the shelves were full of objects. Thousands of them. Pots and statues and bits of jewelry and tools, all with little labels. Things nobody had ever put on display. Things nobody had looked at for a hundred years.

Dr. Amira went to a shelf at the back of the room, and took down something wrapped in a blanket. It was big and flat and round, and when she unwrapped it, it shone so brightly in the light that I had to blink.
A mirror. Made of polished bronze. As big as a bicycle wheel, with a handle carved like a papyrus plant.

"The ancient Egyptians," said Dr. Amira, "used mirrors of polished bronze to bring sunlight deep into tombs, where they were painting the walls. Fire would have made smoke and ruined the paintings. So they stood mirrors at the entrance, and bounced the sunlight down the corridors, from mirror to mirror, all the way to the bottom." She held it up. Our faces shone in it, golden and wobbly. "Reflected sunlight is still sunlight."
Ela gasped. "So we can make the sun stand between his paws! With a mirror! Any time we want!"
"Exactly," said Dr. Amira. She looked very pleased with herself. "A little bit crazy, yes?"
"Can we borrow it?" said Uncle Tarık. "Is that allowed?"
Dr. Amira looked at the mirror. She looked at the door marked DANGER: DO NOT ENTER. She looked at Uncle Tarık.
"It's been in this room for eighty years," she said. "I don't think anyone will notice if it goes for a little walk."
We were halfway back up the stairs, with Bora carrying the mirror wrapped in its blanket, when the lights went out.
Not just in the stairway. Everywhere. The whole museum went dark, all at once, with a soft *clunk.* The air conditioning stopped humming. Somewhere far away, a tourist screamed.
And it got cold.
In Cairo. In a building with no air conditioning. In the middle of the afternoon. It got cold.
"Oh no," said Ela.
Uncle Tarık turned on his flashlight. Upside down. It lit up his own face from below, like a ghost story. He turned it around.
At the top of the stairs, standing in the doorway, were three tall shapes. Three men in gray suits. Their fog eyes glowed faintly in the dark.
"Down!" hissed Dr. Amira. "Back down! Quickly!"
We ran back down the stairs, into the basement. Behind us came footsteps, slow and steady and all in step. And the cold, rolling down the stairs ahead of them like water.
"This way!" Dr. Amira led us down another corridor. Then another. Then up a narrow back stairway that came out in a huge dark room on the ground floor.
The room was full of coffins.

Dozens of them. Big painted wooden coffins, shaped like people, lying in glass cases in long rows. Their painted faces stared up at the ceiling with huge black-rimmed eyes. In the beam of Uncle Tarık's flashlight, their gold paint glittered, and their eyes seemed to move.
"The Royal Mummy Room is next door," whispered Dr. Amira. "This is just the coffins. The mummies are next door."
"*Just* the coffins," said Bora faintly. "Great. That's fine. That's totally fine."

We crouched behind a big stone coffin at the end of the room. Behind us, the door creaked open. The cold rolled in. Frost spread across the glass cases, white and feathery, one after another, all along the row, like something was walking slowly down the room, breathing on each one.
I could hear their footsteps. *Tap. Tap. Tap.* Coming closer.
And then Bora did something very strange.
He closed his eyes. And he went very still. And he started to whisper. Not to us. To something else. Something I couldn't see.
"Please," he whispered. "Please, if you're there. If you can hear me. Please help."
"Bora," hissed Ela. "Who are you talking to?"
Bora didn't answer. He was listening.

Then, very softly, from all around the dark room, came a sound. A tiny scratching, rustling sound. Like dry leaves. Like paper. Coming from the coffins. From inside the coffins. From under them, and behind them, and in the cracks between the stones of the floor.
The Grays stopped.
Out of the cracks and the shadows and the gaps under the glass cases came the museum cats.

There are dozens of cats in the Egyptian Museum. Everyone knows that, Dr. Amira told us later. They live in the basement and the gardens and the storerooms, and they've lived there for a hundred years, generations of them, catching mice and sleeping on statues of pharaohs. The guards feed them. The tourists photograph them. Nobody knows how many there are.
That night, there were at least fifty.

They came out of the dark in a silent, slinking river. Black ones and ginger ones and tabby ones and white ones, thin and wild and fierce, with their ears flat and their eyes glowing green in the beam of the flashlight. They poured across the floor toward the Grays. Then they stopped, all together, in a long line, and arched their backs, and hissed.
Fifty cats, hissing at once, in a dark room full of coffins, is the most terrifying sound I have ever heard. Worse than Tepegöz. Worse than the Troll Queen.
The Grays took a step back.
Then the cats attacked.

They didn't hurt the Grays. Not really. They just swarmed them. Up their legs, onto their shoulders, onto their heads, scratching and yowling and tangling in their hair and getting inside their jackets. One Gray went down under a heap of about twenty cats and didn't get up. Another one was spinning around in circles with a big ginger cat wrapped around his face like a furry mask. The third one ran out of the room, very fast, with three cats hanging off the back of his jacket.
"Now!" whispered Dr. Amira. "While they're busy!"

We ran. Out of the coffin room, through a gallery full of statues, past a huge golden mask that glittered in the dark, out of a side door and into the garden, where the sun was shining and the air was hot and the traffic was honking, as if nothing had happened.
We stood there, gasping.
Bora was laughing and crying at the same time.
"Cats," said Ela. "You called *cats.*"

"The ancient Egyptians loved cats," said Bora, wiping his eyes. "They worshipped them. There was a cat goddess. Bastet. I read it on a sign." He looked back at the museum. "I just thought... maybe the cats would remember that someone used to love them. And they'd help."
"They did," said Dr. Amira. She was looking at Bora with an expression I couldn't read. "Child. You are a very unusual young man."
"Thank you," said Bora. "I get that a lot."

chapters.t: Chapter Eight: Meanwhile, at the Gray Tower
p: *Another part of the story that Kuzey heard much later.*
Vex stood in front of his father's desk, with his hands behind his back.
He always stood with his hands behind his back now. So his father wouldn't see them.

"Egypt," said Mordecai Vane. He was looking at the leather map on the table. A star in the desert, glowing gold. "The Keşişleme. The southeast wind. The wind of the sandstorms. Do you know what that wind can do, Vex? In ancient times, it buried a whole army in the desert. Fifty thousand Persian soldiers. They walked into a sandstorm, and they were never seen again." He smiled. "That's the kind of wind I want."
"Yes, Father."
"You'll go to Cairo. Tonight. With the Grays. And this time, you will not lose."
"Yes, Father."
Mordecai looked up from the map. He looked at his son for a long time.
"Show me your hands," he said.
Vex went very still.
"Your hands, Vex."
Slowly, Vex brought his hands out from behind his back. He held them out, palms down, over the map.
The gray had spread. It was past the knuckles now, on every finger. His fingertips were hard and cracked, like old stone. When he moved them, they made a tiny dry clicking sound.

His father looked at them for a long time. He didn't say anything. His face didn't change. Then he reached out with his own stone hand, the right one, the one that was gray all the way to the wrist, and he touched his son's fingers with his own.
Stone on stone.
"It happened to me too," he said quietly. "At your age. When I first started. It hurts. I know."
Vex couldn't speak. His father had never said anything like that to him before. Never.
"It stops hurting," said Mordecai. "After a while. You stop feeling it at all." He took his hand away. "You stop feeling a lot of things. That's the good part."
He turned back to the map.
"Go and pack," he said. "And take your sister. Keep her close. Keep an eye on her."
In the room down the hall, Vera was sitting on her bed with her mother's bracelet in her lap.
She had taken it off for the first time in seven years. It felt strange, her wrist without it. Light. Empty.
She held it up to the window and looked at the little gray stone.
It was cold. Always cold, even after she'd been wearing it all day. She had never noticed that until Iceland. Now she couldn't stop noticing it.
She held it close to her ear. Very close.
And she heard it. Very, very faint. So faint that she could almost have imagined it.
A tiny, steady *click.* Like a clock. Or a heartbeat.
*Click. Click. Click.*
She sat there for a long time, with the bracelet in her lap, listening to it click.
Then, very slowly, she put it back on.

Because it was her mother's. Because her mother had given it to her, two weeks before she died, and said *to keep you safe.* Because it was the only thing she had left of her mother in the whole world.
And because if she took it off, her father would know that she knew.
The next morning, Dr. Amira took us sailing.
"You need to rest," she said firmly. "And you need to think. And the best place in the world to rest and think is on the Nile. Everyone in Egypt knows that."

So we went down to the river, where the little white sailboats were tied up along the bank. They're called feluccas. Small wooden boats with one huge white sail, a triangle, shaped like the wing of a bird. They've been sailing on the Nile in exactly the same way for thousands of years, since the time of the pharaohs.

Our felucca belonged to an old man named Abu Hassan, who had a white beard and a white turban and no front teeth, and who laughed at everything. Dr. Amira said he was her uncle. Bora said everyone in the world is related to someone.
We climbed in and sat on cushions on the wooden deck. Abu Hassan pushed us off from the bank with a long pole. And we drifted out onto the Nile.

It was so quiet. After the honking and shouting of Cairo, the river was like a different world. The water was wide and brown and smooth. Tall palm trees lined the banks. White birds, egrets, stood in the shallows on one leg, very still. On the far side, a boy was swimming with a water buffalo.
Then the wind dropped.
The sail went flat. The felucca stopped moving. We sat in the middle of the river, going nowhere, in the hot sun.
Abu Hassan shrugged and laughed and lay down on the deck with his turban over his face. "No wind," he said, in English. "We wait. Inshallah, it will come."
I looked at the flat white sail.
"Kuzey," said Ela warningly.
"I'll be careful," I said. "I'll ask nicely."

I closed my eyes. The Nile wind was soft and slow and very, very old. It had been blowing up and down this river for millions of years, carrying the boats north and south. It was tired, in the heat of the day. It was resting.
"Excuse me," I said to it. "Sorry to wake you. We'd like to go up the river a little way. Would you mind?"
The Nile wind thought about it. Then it yawned, a long, warm, lazy yawn.
*For a Windborn,* it said. *A little way.*
The sail filled. Slowly. Gently. It curved out, white and round, like a cheek. The felucca began to move. The water rippled along the sides of the boat with a soft chuckling sound.
Abu Hassan sat up and took his turban off his face. He looked at the sail. He looked at the sky. He licked his finger and held it up, to feel the wind. Then he looked at me, and narrowed his eyes.
And then he laughed, a big toothless laugh, and said something in Arabic.
"What did he say?" I asked Dr. Amira.
She was smiling. "He says, 'The boy has a friend in the sky.'"

We sailed up the Nile for an hour. Past palm trees and fields of sugar cane and little villages with mud-brick houses. A heron flew alongside us for a while. Bora talked to it. It said, Bora reported, that the fishing was bad this year and it was very annoyed about it.
And I lay on my back on the cushions, and looked at the sail, and the blue sky, and the white birds, and for a while, I didn't think about anything at all.
Except, at the very end, as we turned back toward the city, I thought about Shu. Standing between the earth and the sky. Holding up the sky with his arms.
Holding it up. Not owning it. Not controlling it. Just holding it, so that everyone could breathe.
I thought that would be a good kind of job to have.
It was Sunday. Which meant, at six o'clock in the evening Cairo time, my parents called.
I sat on the bed in our hotel room with Uncle Tarık's laptop on my knees, and waited, and my stomach went tight, the way it always does now on Sundays.

The call connected. The screen showed the little metal room with the round window. Through the window, white. Snow and ice, forever. My mom and dad squashed together in front of the camera in their huge orange jackets.
"KUZEY!"
Then the screen froze. On my mom, with her mouth wide open, and my dad, with one eye closed, like a pirate.
I waited. Ten seconds. Twenty.
"...so then the penguin came BACK," my dad's voice was saying, when it came back, "and this time it took my *glove!*"
"It's a different penguin," said my mom. "Your father thinks every penguin is the same penguin."
"It's the same penguin. It has a look. A criminal look."
I laughed. I couldn't help it.
Then my mom leaned closer to the camera, and squinted. "Kuzey, where are you? That's not Greece. Is that... is that a *pyramid* out of the window?"
I looked behind me. Through the hotel window, far away, in the evening light, you could see the tips of the pyramids above the roofs of Cairo.
"Uncle Tarık brought us to Egypt," I said. "After Greece. For... um, more history. Very educational."
"*Egypt!*" said my mom. "Tarık took you to *Egypt?* My brother, who gets lost in his own kitchen? Is he there? Put him on!"
Uncle Tarık leaned into the picture, looking guilty. "Hello, sister."
"Egypt, Tarık?"
"It's very educational," said Uncle Tarık weakly.
My mom looked at him for a long time. Then her face softened. "Are they having fun?"
Uncle Tarık looked at me. I looked at him.

"Yes," I said. And it was strange, because it was true. In between the giants and the trolls and the Grays, in between being scared and missing Grandma, we were. Sometimes. Flying carpets. The dolphins. The hot river. The Minotaur eating baklava.
"Good," said my mom. "Good. And Mum? Is she still with her friends? She hasn't answered my emails."
My throat went tight.
*Tell her,* said a little voice inside me. *Tell her everything.*
But she was at the bottom of the world. On the ice. In a little metal room, with a criminal penguin outside. And there was nothing she could do. Nothing at all. Except worry.
"She's okay," I said. "She's... she's busy. She says she's still singing."
My mom smiled. "That sounds like her."
The screen froze again. On my mom smiling.
I looked at it for a long time.
When the call ended, Vera was standing in the doorway. I don't know how long she'd been there.
"You didn't tell her," she said quietly.
"No."
"Why not?"

"Because she'd worry," I said. "And she can't do anything. She's too far away." I closed the laptop. "When Grandma's home, I'll tell her everything. All of it. And Grandma can be there when I tell her. And it'll be a good story then. Not a scary one."
Vera looked at me for a long moment.
"I wish I had a mother to not tell things to," she said.
Then she went away before I could say anything.
That afternoon, we went to Giza.
We had to see the Sphinx in daylight first, Dr. Amira said. We had to look at it properly. Understand it. Make a plan. "You don't walk into a lion's den without first looking at the lion."
But Uncle Tarık insisted on seeing the Great Pyramid first. And nobody could say no to his face.

Up close, the Great Pyramid is not smooth. From far away, it looks like a perfect triangle, smooth and golden. But up close, it's made of steps. Huge stone blocks, each one as big as a car, stacked on top of each other in rows, going up and up and up into the sky, two million three hundred thousand of them. Uncle Tarık told us. Each one weighs as much as two elephants.
"How did they *do* it?" said Bora, staring up. "Without cranes? Without trucks?"

"Nobody is completely sure," said Dr. Amira. "Ramps. Sleds. Water. Thousands and thousands of workers. Twenty years." She smiled. "And a lot of bread and onions. We found the workers' village. We found their bakeries. They ate very well."
"I like these people," said Bora.
You can go inside the Great Pyramid. There's a tunnel in the side, and then a long, narrow passage that goes up and up, inside the stone, to a room in the middle where a king was buried.
Bora looked at the tunnel. It was dark. And very small. And it went up.
Three of his fears. The dark, small places and heights. Well, two and a half.
"I'll wait outside," he said.
"Bora," I said. "You've fought a giant. You've hugged a Minotaur. You've been in an ice cave with twelve trolls."
"Yes," said Bora. "And I didn't like any of those things either."
But he came. Of course he came. He held onto the back of my shirt the whole way up, bent over double in the narrow passage, breathing very fast, saying "I'm fine, I'm fine, I'm fine," on every step.

The passage went up and up, steep and hot and narrow, with a little wooden walkway and handrails. The walls were smooth stone. The air was hot and stuffy and very still. No wind at all. I couldn't hear a single wind in there. It was the first time in weeks that the winds had been silent, and it made me feel strange, like going deaf.
Then the passage opened into the Grand Gallery.

It's a huge, tall, slanting corridor, inside the pyramid, going up into the darkness, with walls made of giant smooth stones, each row sticking out a little further than the one below, so the ceiling is very high and very narrow. Like being inside a giant stone telescope.
And at the top, the King's Chamber.
A plain room. Smooth red granite walls. Nothing on them at all. No paintings. No writing. And at one end, an empty stone box, the king's coffin, with no lid. Just a box.
We stood there, in the middle of the pyramid, in the silence.
"It's empty," said Bora. "Where's the king?"

"Nobody knows," said Dr. Amira. "When the first explorers came in, more than a thousand years ago, it was already empty. Thieves, maybe. Or maybe..." She shrugged. "Maybe it was always empty. Egypt has many secrets."
Then I felt something.
A tiny breath of air. On my cheek. Coming from the wall.

There are two little holes in the walls of the King's Chamber. Small square shafts, as wide as my hand, going up through the stone at an angle, all the way to the outside of the pyramid. The air shafts. One points north. One points south.
The air was coming from the south one. A tiny breath of hot, dry air from the desert outside.
And it was whispering.
*The silver one came here,* it whispered. *She stood where you stand. She listened, as you listen. And then she went to the lion. Go to the lion, little Windborn. The lion is waiting.*
The Sphinx is bigger than you think.

It's carved from the rock of the desert itself. Not built, like the pyramids. *Carved,* out of the stone of the ground, like a sculpture made from a mountain. A lion, lying down, as long as a football field, with its huge paws stretched out in front of it. And the head of a pharaoh, wearing the striped headdress of a king.

Its nose is broken off. Its face is worn by thousands of years of wind and sand. Its body is crumbling in places, and patched with newer stones. But its eyes still look straight out at the sunrise, calm and patient, as if it's waiting for something.
"It's waiting for us," I said. I didn't know why I said it.
The wind whispered around its paws. *Yes. Yes. Yes.*

There were tourists everywhere. And guards, in white uniforms. And men selling postcards and little plastic pyramids and scarves. And camel drivers, with camels covered in colorful blankets and tassels, shouting "Very good price! Very good camel! Camel ride, my friend! Very cheap!" at everyone.
One camel was standing right next to Bora. It was tall and brown and very scruffy, with long eyelashes and a big lower lip. It was making grumbly noises, deep in its throat. *Grrrrumph. Grrrrumph.*
Bora looked at it. Then his face changed.
"He says," Bora reported, "his name is Mustafa. And he hates tourists. And he wants a carrot."
Mustafa's owner, a young man with a big smile, was shouting at another tourist. He hadn't noticed.
"Does he know anything about the Sphinx?" Ela asked.
"Ela, he's a camel."
"He's a camel who lives *next to* the Sphinx," said Ela. "He's here every day. He's probably seen more of the Sphinx than any person alive. Ask him."
Bora asked. He did it quietly, standing very close to Mustafa's big hairy shoulder, and the camel bent his long neck down, so his huge head was right next to Bora's.
The camel grumbled for a long time. A long, low, complaining sort of grumble, with lots of snorts in it. Bora nodded and nodded.

"He says," Bora translated, "that tourists are very stupid and always want photos, and they are too heavy, especially the Americans. He says his owner is a good man but sings very badly. He says the food is terrible. He says..." Bora frowned. "He says that every night, after the tourists go home, the guards leave, and the sand between the lion's paws moves on its own."
We all went quiet.
"He says the camels never go near there," said Bora. "Never. Not even the young stupid ones. Because something underneath the sand breathes."
"Breathes," I repeated.
Mustafa grumbled again. Bora listened.
"He says," Bora said, "it breathes hot. Like the desert at noon. And on some nights it whispers. In a language even the oldest camels don't know."
I looked at the Sphinx. At the space between its paws, where a little stone temple stood, half buried in the sand. Where the tourists were taking photos and eating ice cream.
"Then we come back tonight," I said.
"With a mirror," said Dr. Amira.
"But we can't come at sunset," said Ela. "The sun won't be in the right place. And it'll be full of tourists. And after sunset, there's no sun at all. So how..."
"Ah," said Dr. Amira. "We don't come at sunset. We come at midnight."
"Midnight?" said Bora. "There's no sun at midnight!"

"No," said Dr. Amira, smiling her little secret smile. "But there is the moon. And the moon," she said, "is only the sun's mirror. All the light of the moon is sunlight, bouncing off it. Reflected sunlight is still sunlight." She looked up at the sky, where the pale ghost of the moon was already rising over the desert. "And tonight, the moon is full."
§CLUE The moon is only the sun's mirror. Reflected sunlight is still sunlight. (Dr. Amira.)
Bora gave Mustafa the carrot from his lunch box. Mustafa ate it in one crunch, and made a sound that Bora said was the camel version of "Thank you, you are the only human who has ever understood me."
Then he sat down. Right on top of Mustafa's owner's foot. And refused to get up for twenty minutes.
"See?" said Uncle Tarık, with deep satisfaction. "They *do* sit on people."
At midnight, the Giza plateau was empty and silver.

The full moon hung over the pyramids, so bright that it threw sharp black shadows across the sand. The three pyramids stood against the starry sky like giant silver triangles. The desert stretched away behind them, silver and black, forever. The city of Cairo glowed orange on the horizon, and you could hear it, very faintly, honking, even now. But here, at the pyramids, it was silent except for the hot, whispering wind.

Dr. Amira knew a guard who owed her a favor. She didn't tell us what the favor was. He was an old man with a big gray mustache, and he let us through a little side gate, and then very carefully turned around and looked the other way, at a wall, and started whistling.
We walked across the sand toward the Sphinx.
In the moonlight, its face looked alive.

During the day, with the tourists and the noise and the camels, it had looked like a statue. A huge, old, broken statue. But at night, in the silver light, with the shadows filling in the cracks and the missing nose, it looked like a real face. Calm. Patient. Wise. Watching us come toward it with its great blank eyes.

Bora was carrying the bronze mirror, wrapped in its blanket. Uncle Tarık had his umbrella. Ela had the Clue Book and a flashlight. Dr. Amira had a bag full of things she said might be useful, which turned out to be a lot of bottles of water and a packet of biscuits.
We stopped in front of the Sphinx, in the sand, between its giant stone paws.
"Now," said Dr. Amira quietly. "Bora. The mirror."

Bora unwrapped the big bronze mirror. It shone in the moonlight, silver-gold, like a second moon. He held it up with both hands, and we all helped him tilt it, slowly, slowly, until it caught the light of the full moon and threw a bright spot of silver light onto the sand in front of us.
Then, very slowly, we moved the spot across the ground. Across the sand. Toward the Sphinx. Between its paws. Past the little stone temple. Up to the great stone chest of the lion.
Until it rested exactly between the giant paws.
Nothing happened.
We stood there, holding the heavy mirror, our arms aching, the silver spot of light shaking a little on the sand.
"Maybe the moon doesn't count," whispered Bora. "Maybe it has to be the real sun."
"Wait," I said.
Because I could feel it. Under my feet. A breath. A slow, deep, hot breath, coming up through the sand. In. And out. In. And out.
Something underneath the sand was breathing.
And the sand began to move.

chapters.t: Chapter Fourteen: The Face in the Sand
p: It started in the middle of the silver spot of light.

The sand began to flow. Not blow. *Flow.* Like water running down a drain. It poured away from the place between the paws, in a slow, hissing spiral, around and around and down, into some hole we couldn't see. More and more sand. The spiral got wider, and deeper, and the hissing got louder, like a huge snake.
And under the sand, something appeared.
A stone slab. Flat and smooth and very old, lying in the ground between the paws. And carved into it, a face.

The same face as the Sphinx. The same striped headdress. The same calm, wide eyes. But this face had its nose. This face was perfect. As if it had been hidden under the sand for five thousand years, waiting, and the wind and time had never touched it.
The sand stopped flowing.
We stood around the stone face, very still, the mirror still shining down on it.
Then its eyes opened.
They were made of light.
Golden light, warm and bright, like the sun at noon. They glowed up at us out of the stone. And they *looked* at us. One by one. At Uncle Tarık. At Dr. Amira. At Ela. At Bora. And then at me.
"Who wakes the guardian?"

The voice was deep and ancient, and it came from everywhere at once. From the sand, from the stone, from the great stone lion itself, rising above us into the stars. It made the ground hum. It made my bones hum.
"Who walks the old road by moonlight?"
My mouth was dry. I couldn't speak. Ela elbowed me in the ribs.

"Kuzey Aydın," I said. My voice came out as a squeak. I cleared my throat and tried again. "Kuzey Aydın. Windborn. Of the Order of the Compass Rose. Grandson of Nermin Aydın. I came for the Keşişleme."
"Ah."
The golden eyes looked at me for a long time.

"The silver-haired woman's boy," said the voice, and it sounded almost pleased. Almost warm. "She came here, forty years ago, by the light of a full moon, like you. She sat on my paw and talked to me all night. She told me many stories. She told me about a boy who would come one day. A boy who would hear the wind." The light in the eyes flickered. "I have been waiting for you, Kuzey Aydın."
"Thank you," I said, because I didn't know what else to say.
"Then you know the rule," said the Sphinx.
"Um," I said. "No?"

"Three questions," said the Sphinx. "One for each of you who stands before me and is young. The old ones may watch." Its eyes moved to Uncle Tarık and Dr. Amira, then back to the three of us. "Answer all three, and the wind is yours. Fail one..."
The sand under our feet trembled.
"And you will stay here with me," said the Sphinx. "Forever. As sand."
Bora made a small noise.
"Three?" he whispered. "I thought there were two riddles."
"Two riddles," said the Sphinx. "And one question. You will see."
"The first riddle," said the Sphinx, "every child knows."
Its golden eyes turned to Ela.
"What walks on four legs in the morning, two legs in the afternoon, and three legs in the evening?"
Ela didn't even blink.

"A human," she said immediately. "A baby crawls on four legs, in the morning of its life. A grown-up walks on two, in the afternoon. And an old person walks with a cane, in the evening. That's three."
The golden eyes looked at her for a long moment.

"Correct," said the Sphinx. "That one is free. Every child in the world has been told the answer. It is a test of nothing. Except whether you listen to stories." Its voice grew a little warmer. "You listen to stories. That is good."
Ela pushed her glasses up her nose and looked very, very pleased.
"But you did not answer it the way the Greek hero did," said the Sphinx. "He said only, *Man.* One word. You told me why. That is better. Knowing *why* is always better."
"I'm going to write that down," said Ela, and she did.
The sand under our feet stopped trembling. Just a little.
"Now," said the Sphinx.
Its golden eyes turned slowly toward me.

"The second," it said. "The one no one has ever answered. For five thousand years, they have come. Kings. Priests. Philosophers. Thieves. Generals. Scholars from every land. They asked for my second riddle, because they had heard the stories. And every single one of them answered wrong." The golden light flickered. "Every one."
"What happened to them?" I asked. My voice was very small.
The Sphinx said nothing. But the sand under my feet seemed suddenly very soft. Very fine. Like it was made of something that had once been something else.
I tried not to think about it.
"Are you ready, Windborn?"
No, I thought.
"Yes," I said.
The Sphinx spoke slowly, and every word fell into the silence like a stone into a deep well.
*I have no voice, but I can shout.*
*I have no hands, but I can push.*
*I can never be seen, but I can be felt.*
*You can never hold me, but you can follow me.*
*I am older than the pyramids, and I am born new every morning.*
*What am I?*

§CLUE I have no voice, but I can shout. I have no hands, but I can push. I can never be seen, but I can be felt. You can never hold me, but you can follow me. I am older than the pyramids, and I am born new every morning. What am I?
The silence after it went on and on. The moon shone down. The mirror trembled in Bora's hands.

Ela opened her mouth. Then closed it. I could see her thinking. Her eyes were moving fast behind her glasses, flicking back and forth, the way they do when she's working out a code. *Time? A ghost? A shadow? A thought?* None of them fit. Not all of it.
Bora scratched his head with one hand, the mirror wobbling.
Uncle Tarık and Dr. Amira looked at each other. Dr. Amira's lips were moving, very slightly. I think she was trying out answers in Arabic.
And I started to laugh.

I couldn't help it. It came bubbling up from inside me, out of nowhere. Out of all three of my winds. The North Wind was laughing, and the Black Wind was laughing, and I was laughing, standing in the sand in front of the Sphinx in the middle of the night, with my hand over my mouth, trying to stop.
"Kuzey!" hissed Ela, horrified. "This is *not* the time!"
But it was so obvious.

It had been obvious my whole life. Every day. Every time a door slammed in our apartment. Every time the seagulls gave up flying and sat on the lamp posts. Every time I lost my hat on the ferry. It was so obvious that nobody could see it. Like looking for your glasses when they're on your head.
"The wind," I said. "You're describing the wind."
*No voice, but it can shout.* A storm.
*No hands, but it can push.* A sail. A door. A ship.
*Never seen, but felt.* On your face. In your hair.
*Never held, but followed.* Like a sailor follows it. Like a kite.
*Older than the pyramids. Born new every morning.* The first breeze of the day.
The Sphinx was silent.

It was silent for so long that I stopped laughing. Then I started to worry. Then I started to really, really worry. The sand under my feet felt soft. The golden eyes didn't move. They didn't blink. They just stared at me.
Then, very slowly, the light in them grew brighter.
"Five thousand years," said the Sphinx.
Its voice was different now. Quieter. Almost a whisper.

"Five thousand years, and every scholar, every king, every thief who came here answered with clever words. *Time.* *Thought.* *Death.* *The soul.* *The voice of the gods.* Long, clever answers. Beautiful answers. Wrong answers. Not one of them answered with the simplest truth. Because not one of them could hear the wind. They were too busy being clever to listen."
The golden eyes looked at me.
"Correct, Windborn."

Ela grabbed my hand and squeezed it so hard that it hurt. Bora let out a breath so big that the mirror wobbled and the silver spot of light jumped around the sand. Uncle Tarık sat down very suddenly. Dr. Amira was laughing, quietly, with tears in her eyes.
"Never," she whispered. "Never in my whole life. I never thought of it."
"Nobody does," said the Sphinx. "That is the point of it."
"Now," said the Sphinx. "The third question."
Its golden eyes turned, slowly, toward Bora.
"This one is not a riddle," said the Sphinx. "It is a choice. And it is for you, Beastspeaker."
Bora's mouth fell open. "How do you know I'm a..."

"The cats of Cairo told me," said the Sphinx. "Cats have been telling me things for five thousand years. They are terrible gossips." The golden light flickered, the way a smile might. "Listen carefully, Beastspeaker."
Bora swallowed.

"The wind of the southeast," said the Sphinx, "is wild. The wildest of the seven. In ancient times, it brought the great sandstorms. Storms that turned day into night. Storms that buried whole cities. Whole armies. The army of the Persian king Cambyses, fifty thousand men, walked into the western desert, and the wind of the southeast rose up and covered them, and they were never seen again. Their bones are still out there, under the sand. Somewhere."
The wind around us hissed and whispered.
"If the Windborn takes this wind," said the Sphinx, "it will be his to command. A wind that can bury armies. Should he?"
Bora looked at me.
Then at the Sphinx.

Then he did something I didn't expect. Bora, who always says the first thing that comes into his head. Bora, who once answered a math question in class with "pizza" because he was thinking about lunch.
He *thought about it.*
Really thought. For a long time. Standing in the sand, holding the heavy mirror, with his forehead wrinkled and his lips pressed together. The moonlight shining on his face.
We waited. Nobody said anything. Nobody helped him. It was his question.
"No," he said finally.
The golden eyes didn't move.

"I don't think anyone should *command* it," said Bora slowly. "Not even Kuzey. And Kuzey's my best friend, and he's the best person I know." He frowned, working it out. "Kuzey told the Black Wind he would set all the winds free one day. When it's over. I was there. I heard him." He took a breath. "So I think the Keys should be *protected.* So the bad guy can't use them. So nobody can bury any more armies. But not commanded. Because the wind isn't a pet. It's not a thing you own. It's... it's a *someone.*"
He looked over at the edge of the plateau, where, in the moonlight, I could just see a scruffy brown shape standing by the camel drivers' tents, watching us.
"Even Mustafa isn't a pet," said Bora. "He told me. He works with his owner. He's not *owned* by him. There's a difference. Mustafa says it's the most important difference in the world."
The sand stopped trembling.
For a long time, the Sphinx said nothing at all. The golden eyes rested on Bora. The moon shone. The wind whispered.
"A Beastspeaker," said the Sphinx softly, "who understands that no creature is a possession. Not a camel. Not a cat. Not a wind."
The light in its eyes grew warm. Warm like the sun.
"The silver-haired woman," said the Sphinx, "chose her friends well."

chapters.t: Chapter Eighteen: The Hall of Scarabs
p: The stone face sank into the sand.

Slowly. With a long, deep, grinding sound, like a giant door closing. Down, and down, until it was gone. And where it had been, a staircase appeared. Stone steps, going down into the earth, under the paws of the Sphinx.
Into golden darkness.

And from the bottom of the stairs came a breath of hot, wild wind. It smelled of spices. Cinnamon and cumin and pepper. And sand. And faraway deserts, deserts I'd never seen, where nobody had ever walked.
"Thank you," I said to the Sphinx.

*Go, little Windborn,* said the great stone lion above us. Its voice was very soft now, fading, like it was going back to sleep. *And when you see the silver-haired woman again, tell her I still remember the stories. Tell her to come back and tell me more.*
"I will," I said.
We went down the stairs.

They led into a long hall. The walls were painted. Every centimeter of them, from the floor to the ceiling, in bright colors that looked like they had been painted yesterday. Blue and green and red and gold.

There were people sailing boats on the Nile, with white sails, like Abu Hassan's felucca. There were birds flying over marshes. Fish swimming. Farmers cutting wheat. And across the ceiling, the sun god Ra, with the head of a falcon and a red sun on his head, riding across the sky in a golden boat.
And everywhere, painted in the spaces between the pictures, were little blue beetles.
Scarabs. Hundreds of them. Thousands of them. Painted bright blue, with their legs and their shiny wing cases, in neat rows along the walls. Like a border on a carpet.

"The scarab," whispered Dr. Amira, "was sacred to the Egyptians. They believed a giant scarab beetle rolled the sun across the sky every day, the way a real scarab rolls a ball of dung across the ground." She looked at the beetles. "They were symbols of rebirth. Of new life."
At the far end of the hall, on a golden pedestal shaped like a rising sun, lay a bronze needle.
It glowed the color of sand at sunset. Orange and gold and pink, shifting and moving, like a desert in the evening light.
The Keşişleme Key.
"Careful," said Dr. Amira quietly. "In tombs, nothing is just decoration."
She was right.
As soon as I took a step toward the pedestal, the painted scarabs on the walls began to move.
At first I thought I was imagining it. The painted legs twitched. The painted wing cases shivered.
Then they peeled off the plaster. And became real.

Thousands of blue beetles, as big as my thumb, shiny and hard, with clicking legs and buzzing wings, peeling off the walls and the ceiling and pouring down onto the floor. A waterfall of beetles. A blue, clicking, buzzing carpet, spreading across the floor between us and the Key.
"Bora!" I yelled. "Can you talk to beetles?"
"I've never tried!" Bora put down the mirror. He closed his eyes and concentrated so hard that his face went red. His hands were in fists. "They're saying... they're saying..."
"WHAT?"
"'Guard. Guard. Guard. Guard.'" Bora opened his eyes. "That's it! That's all they say! Over and over! They're not very good at conversation!"
The beetles swarmed toward us. Clicking and buzzing. Some of them flew, whirring past our heads. One landed in Ela's hair and she screamed for the first time in this whole adventure.
"Kuzey!" she shouted, pulling it out. "Get the Key! We'll hold them back!"
"How?"
"I don't know! We'll think of something!"

Uncle Tarık opened his giant umbrella with a *whoomp* and started sweeping the beetles back with it, like a broom. Dr. Amira was throwing bottles of water at them. Bora was still talking to them, saying "Please, please stop, we're the good guys, the Sphinx said we could, please." Ela was stamping her feet, being careful not to squash any, which is very hard to do with thousands of beetles.
I ran.

The beetles crunched under my feet. I felt terrible about it, but there was no other way. They crawled up my legs. Into my shoes. Up my back. Into my hair. Clicking and buzzing in my ears. *Guard. Guard. Guard.* I couldn't see the pedestal anymore. I couldn't see anything but blue.
I reached out blindly.
My hand hit something hard and warm. The pedestal.
I grabbed the Keşişleme Key.

chapters.t: Chapter Twenty: The Wind of the Sandstorms
p: Hot wind exploded out of it.

A real sandstorm. Right there in the tomb. Golden sand, whirling around me, so thick I couldn't see anything at all. It roared in my ears. It stung my face. It filled my mouth and my nose and my eyes. It was the hottest, driest, wildest thing I had ever felt. Like standing in the middle of the Sahara in a hurricane.
And in the middle of the storm, there was a voice.
It was dry and laughing, cunning and quick. Like an old trader in a bazaar. Like someone who has sold carpets for a thousand years and always, always gets the best price.
*So!* it said. *So, so, so! The boy who answered the riddle! The boy who laughed at the Sphinx! Ha!*
"Hello," I said, through a mouthful of sand.

*Hello, hello, little Windborn!* The storm swirled around me, faster and faster. *Fifty thousand Persians I buried, you know. Fifty thousand! In one afternoon! The kings loved me for that. The kings always loved me.* The voice dropped to a whisper, right in my ear. *Will you command me, little Windborn? Will you send me to bury your enemies? The cold man with the stone hand? His son? His gray men? I could do it. One word from you. They would never be seen again.*
For one second, I thought about it.
I thought about Mordecai, with his too-many-teeth smile. About Grandma in her cold tower. About Uncle Tarık, frozen to the floor in Crete. About the Grays, with their fog eyes.
One word.
Then I thought about Vex. Standing in the dark behind the trolls. I didn't know about his hands then. But I remembered his face, on Galata Tower, trying so hard to look bigger than he was.
And I thought about Vera. Waving from the street in Athens. Smiling at the ravens.
And I thought about the Black Wind. *I sank a hundred ships for them. Boys no older than you.*
"No," I said. "No. I won't send you to bury anyone. I'll protect you. Until you can be free. Like I promised the Black Wind. Like I promised all of you."
The storm went quiet. Just for a second. The sand hung in the air around me, frozen, like a photograph.
*Free?* said the trader's voice.
*Hah!*
The storm swirled again. But it was laughing now. Really laughing, a big, dry, delighted laugh.
*Then let us be friends, little Windborn! For now! Friends! I have not had a friend in four thousand years. Kings, I have had. Generals. Never a friend.*
The sandstorm shot outward and swept the whole hall.

But it didn't hurt anyone. It didn't hurt the beetles. It picked them up, very gently, thousands of them, off the floor and off my friends and out of Ela's hair, and it carried them back to the walls. And it stuck them back onto the plaster, one by one, each one in its exact place, where it froze and became a painting again. Blue and shiny and perfectly still. Every single one. Back in its row.
Then the sand settled.
The hall was quiet again. The painted boats sailed on the painted Nile. The painted sun god rode across the painted sky. The scarabs sat in their neat blue rows.
And the Keşişleme Key sank into my palm, warm as the desert sun at noon.

Three winds inside me now. North. Black. Southeast. The cold one, the stormy one and the hot one. I could feel them talking to each other, inside my chest, like new kids meeting at a lunch table on the first day of school. The North Wind was being polite. The Black Wind was being suspicious. The Keşişleme was telling them both a very long story about a camel it had once known.
When I breathed out, my breath came out as a little puff of golden sand. It sparkled in the light.
"Kuzey," said Bora quietly.
He was pointing behind me, up the stairs.
"We have company."
Vex Vane stood at the top of the stairs, outlined against the moonlight.

No Grays this time. Just Vex. He looked thinner than in Iceland. Paler. There were dark circles under his eyes. He was wearing his gray gloves, and he was holding them strangely, a little away from his body, as if they hurt.
And in front of him, with his gray-gloved hand on her shoulder, stood Ela.

I hadn't even seen him grab her. She must have run back up the stairs as soon as the sandstorm settled, to make sure the way out was still open. That's what Ela does. She checks the exits. She always checks the exits.
This time, someone had been waiting at the exit.
"Three to one," said Vex.
His voice was strange. Tight. Like a wire about to snap.
"That's not good enough for Father," he said. "Two to one, he was angry. Three to one..." He laughed, but it wasn't a laugh at all. "Do you know what he does when I fail, Windborn? Do you?"
"Let her go," I said.
I walked slowly up the stairs toward them. Bora was right behind me. Uncle Tarık was behind him, his umbrella raised. Dr. Amira was behind him, holding a bottle of water like a weapon.
"Stop," said Vex. "Stop there. Or I'll freeze her."
We stopped.

"Give me one Key," said Vex. "Just one. Any one. I don't care which. The new one. The sand one. Give it to me, and I'll let her go, and I'll go back, and he won't..." He stopped. His jaw was tight. "Just give me one."
His hand tightened on Ela's shoulder. Frost crept down her sleeve. White and feathery. Down her arm, to her elbow, to her wrist.
Ela didn't scream.

She didn't even shiver. She just stood there and glared at him, the way she glares at a math problem she can't solve yet. A very furious, very determined glare, the glare of someone who has never in her life given up on a problem, and isn't going to start now.
"I can't," I said. "I can't give you a Key. They're inside me. They're part of me now."
"Then *you* come with me," said Vex. "Father can take them out. He knows how. He's read about it. In the old book." His face twisted. "It'll hurt a lot, I think."
"Vex," I said. "Look at your hands."
He flinched. As if I had hit him.

I didn't know what I was looking at, then. Not really. But I could see that he held his hands strangely. That the fingers of the gloves were stiff. That when he moved them, they made a tiny sound. Like pebbles.
"Don't," he said. "Don't look at them. Don't talk about them."
"Vex."
It wasn't me.
It was Vera.
She came up the outside of the stairs, behind her brother. Quietly, in the moonlight. She was wearing a dark dress, and her pale hair was tied back. On her wrist, the silver bracelet glinted.
"Let her go," she said quietly.
Vex didn't turn around.
"Go back to the car, Vera."
"No."
"*Go back to the car.*"
"No," said Vera.

She stepped closer. She was standing right behind him now. In the moonlight, the twins looked so alike. The same pale hair. The same sharp faces. But Vex's face was hard and frightened and angry. And Vera's was very calm.
"I'm done, Vex," she said. "I'm done being cold. I'm done watching Father hurt people. Grandma Nermin. The professor. Kuzey. *You.*"
"He doesn't hurt me."

"He's turning you into stone," said Vera. "Slowly. Finger by finger. And he doesn't even care." Her voice cracked, just a little. "And you're done too. I know you are. I hear you crying at night, when you think I'm asleep."
Vex's whole body went stiff.
For a moment, his face looked about seven years old. A little boy. A little boy standing on a beach on a Sunday, with his father telling stories and doing the voices.
His hand on Ela's shoulder loosened. Just a little.
And Ela stomped on his foot as hard as she could.

She's small, but she's fierce, and she was wearing hiking boots. Vex yelped and let go. Ela dived down the stairs toward me. I caught her. Bora caught both of us. We all fell over in a heap at the bottom of the steps.
Vex spun around. He raised his gray hand. Not at us. At his sister. His face was furious and broken, both at the same time.
"You *traitor,*" he hissed. "You traitor! He'll know! He'll know you helped them! He'll know everything!"
Vera didn't move. She looked at her brother's raised gray hand. Then she looked at his face.
"Then let him know," she said.
Vex's hand was shaking. Frost was building on his fingers. White fog curled around them.
For a long, long moment, the twins stood there on the stairs, in the moonlight, under the great stone face of the Sphinx. Brother and sister. His hand raised. Her hands at her sides.
He didn't do it.
He couldn't. Whatever he was, whatever his father was making him into, he couldn't freeze his sister.
But he didn't lower his hand either.
I didn't wait.

I had three winds inside me now. And all three of them were angry. Angry on Ela's behalf. The North Wind was cold with anger. The Black Wind was crackling with it. And the Keşişleme, the new one, the trader, was hot and dry and quiet, the most dangerous kind of angry.
*Shall I bury him?* it whispered. *Just a little? Just up to his neck?*
"No," I said. "But you can move him. Gently. Very gently. A long way away."
*Ha! Gently!* said the Keşişleme. *I have never done anything gently in my life. But for you, little friend, I will try.*
I let it out.

A sandstorm rose up out of the ground. Not a big one. Not a cruel one. A big, round, golden whirlwind of sand, glittering in the moonlight. It lifted Vex off his feet, very gently, like a giant hand picking up a kitten. It carried him up into the air, spinning slowly, his arms and legs waving.
"PUT ME DOWN!" Vex shouted. "PUT ME DOWN! YOU CAN'T DO THIS! FATHER WILL..."

The sandstorm carried him across the plateau. Past the Sphinx's paw. Past the little temple. Past the line of camels, who all turned their heads to watch him go by. Mustafa made a loud grumbling noise that Bora said was laughter. Across the sand, up the hill, all the way to the car park on the far side.
And there, very gently, it set him down on the roof of his own big black car.
Right in the middle. Sitting cross-legged. With sand in his hair.
He sat there, completely still, in the moonlight, looking very small.
Then the sandstorm came back to me, and settled down inside me, purring like a cat that has caught a mouse.
*Gently,* it said, very pleased with itself. *Very gently. Was that gentle enough, little friend?*
"That was perfect," I said.
"That," said Bora, from the heap at the bottom of the stairs, "was the most satisfying thing I have ever seen."

chapters.t: Chapter Twenty-Four: Koshari at Four in the Morning
p: Vera sat on the bottom step of the stairs, shaking.
She had her arms wrapped around her knees, and she was staring at the sand. Her face was very white. On her wrist, the silver bracelet glinted in the moonlight.
"I can't go back now," she said, very quietly. "I can't ever go back. Father will know. Vex will tell him."
I didn't know what to say.

Ela did. She got up from the heap at the bottom of the stairs, brushing sand off her clothes. Her shoulder was still frosty where Vex had held it. She walked over to Vera and sat down beside her on the step. Not too close. The way you'd sit down next to a stray cat, that you don't want to frighten away.
"Then don't go back," said Ela. "Come with us. For real this time."
Vera looked at her. "You don't trust me. You've never trusted me. I know you haven't. I've seen you watching me."

"I don't," said Ela honestly. Ela is always honest. It's one of her best and worst things. "Not completely. I'm at about eighty-five percent." She looked down at her frosty shoulder, then back at Vera. "But you just saved me. You stood up to your brother. For me. So I'm going to try for a hundred."
"Ela trusts nobody," Bora explained, sitting down on Vera's other side. "It took her two years to trust me. Two *years.* And I'm very trustworthy. I gave a raven my cheese sandwich."
Vera laughed.
It came out like a hiccup. Surprised, as if she hadn't laughed in a long, long time, and had forgotten how it was supposed to sound.

Dr. Amira came and knelt in front of her in the sand. She looked into Vera's face with her kind, sharp eyes. She looked at how thin she was. At the dark circles under her eyes, just like her brother's.
"Child," she said, "are you hungry?"
Vera nodded.
"Then first we eat," said Dr. Amira firmly, standing up and brushing the sand off her knees. "Then we talk. That is the Egyptian way. Nobody can talk properly on an empty stomach."
We ate koshari at four in the morning, in a tiny restaurant near the Nile, with fluorescent lights and plastic tables, that was open all night for taxi drivers.

Koshari is the most Egyptian food there is, Dr. Amira said. It's rice, lentils and little macaroni, all mixed together in one bowl, with chickpeas, and crispy fried onions on top, and a spicy tomato sauce, and a garlic vinegar sauce. It sounds strange. It's the best thing in the world.
Bora had three bowls.
Vera had two, very fast, without looking up, as if she hadn't eaten properly in a long time. As if she was afraid someone would take it away.
Nobody asked her anything until she was finished. Dr. Amira wouldn't let us.

When she was done, she put down her spoon and sat back and looked at us. All of us. Ela with the Clue Book. Bora with his third bowl. Uncle Tarık with sand in his hair. Dr. Amira with her glasses on their chain. And me.
She took a deep breath.
"Okay," she said. "I'll tell you everything I know."

"The gray tower," said Vera, "is on an island. A small one, just a rock, really, in the sea, far in the north. Near Scotland, I think, or Norway. I've never seen a map with it on. The fog is always there. Ships can't see it. Planes can't see it. My father made the fog, years ago, with the gray hand. It never goes away."
"How do you get there?" asked Ela, writing.

"Through the fog," said Vera. "My father can travel through it. Fog roads, he calls them. Any fog, anywhere in the world, connects to the fog around the tower, if you know how. He can step into a fog in Athens and step out of the fog at the tower. He takes us with him, sometimes. And the Grays." She shivered. "It's horrible. It's so cold. Like being frozen and then unfrozen."
"And Grandma?" I said. "Is she okay?"
Vera's face softened.

"She's okay," she said. "She's in a room at the top of the tower. It's cold, and it's lonely, but she's okay. She sings. All day. Old songs, in Turkish. And she talks to my father every day. He goes up and sees her every single evening, and she talks to him. About old times. About when he was her student." She looked down at her hands. "I listen at the door, sometimes. I think... I think she's the only person he really talks to. Even though she's his prisoner."
I didn't say anything. I couldn't.

"She was kind to me," said Vera. "When I brought her food, once. She asked me about my school. My favorite books. She asked me what I wanted to be when I grew up." Vera's voice wobbled. "Nobody ever asked me that before."
Ela had stopped writing.
"What do you want to be?" she asked quietly.
Vera looked surprised. Then she smiled a little.
"A marine biologist," she said. "I want to study the sea. Whales and dolphins. My mother loved the sea."
"Kuzey's parents are marine biologists," said Bora. "They're in Antarctica right now. Counting penguins."
Vera looked at me with her strange green eyes. "Really?"
"Really," I said. "A penguin stole my dad's hat."
Vera laughed again. It was getting easier for her. You could tell.
Then her face went serious.

"There's something else," she said. "Something important. My father only has one Key. The Lodos, from Crete. He doesn't have the Keys inside him, like you. He can't. He's not a Windborn. He has to hold it in his stone hand, all the time. And the Lodos fights him. Every second. It's cracking his hand. I've seen it. There are new cracks every day."
She took a deep breath.

"But he has spent years studying the old maps. And he thinks he knows where the next Key is. Before the star even lights up on the map. He's found it in the old books. The Gündoğusu. The East Wind. The wind of the sunrise."
She looked at me.
"It's in Japan. Near Mount Fuji. And this time, he's not sending Vex. He's going there himself."
"Himself?" I said. "Not Vex?"
"He doesn't trust Vex anymore," said Vera quietly. "Not after Iceland. Not after tonight." She looked down at the silver bracelet on her wrist, turning it slowly. "And he doesn't trust me at all."
On the first morning after the Sphinx, Bora said he had to go back to the museum.
"To thank the cats," he said. "They saved us. You have to say thank you. My grandmother says if someone helps you and you don't say thank you, a little bit of your heart goes cold."

So he went, with Dr. Amira, carrying a big bag of dried fish from the market. Ela and I went too. We waited in the garden of the museum, by a pond with lotus flowers in it, while Bora sat on the grass under a palm tree, opened the bag and waited.

They came in ones and twos at first. A thin black cat with one ear. A ginger one with a crooked tail. A tiny gray kitten, who walked straight up to Bora and climbed into his lap. Then more. And more. Out of the bushes, off the walls, through the railings, from under the statues. Until Bora was sitting in a circle of about forty cats, all eating fish, all purring.
It was the loudest purring I have ever heard. It sounded like a motorbike.
Bora talked to them for a long time. Sometimes he laughed. Sometimes he nodded seriously. Once he said, "No, I'm sorry, I can't take you to Turkey. My mom already has a cat. A very jealous one."
Then his face changed.
He stood up very carefully, so as not to disturb the kitten, which was asleep in his hood, and came over to us.

"The cats say," he said quietly, "that the gray men are watching our hotel. Two of them. Day and night. One by the front door, pretending to read a newspaper. One on the roof across the street." He glanced back at the cats. "And they say the gray men always know which way we go. Even when we take the back door. Even when we go in a taxi. The cats think it's very strange. They say it's like the gray men can smell us."
Ela frowned. "That's what I've been saying. How do they always know?"
"We'll move," said Dr. Amira firmly. "Tonight. To my house. I have three spare beds and a very large sofa."
"They'll find us there too," said Ela. "They always find us."
Nobody had an answer to that.
The little gray kitten woke up in Bora's hood and mewed.
"She says," said Bora, "she wants to come with us."
"Bora," said Ela.

"I *know,*" said Bora sadly. He lifted the kitten out of his hood, very gently, and held her up so their noses touched. "I'm sorry," he told her. "But you have to stay here. You have to guard the pharaohs. It's an important job. Your great-great-great-great-grandmother did it."
The kitten looked at him with big yellow eyes. Then she licked his nose.
He put her down, and she ran back to the others, and they all sat in a row on the wall of the museum and watched us go.

"Bastet's children," said Dr. Amira softly, watching them. "That's what we used to call them. The cats of Egypt. The children of the cat goddess." She looked at Bora. "The old Egyptians believed that cats could see things humans could not. Spirits. Gods. The truth about people." She smiled. "I think they're right. They certainly see something in you."

chapters.t: Chapter Twenty-Seven: Meanwhile, at the Gray Tower
p: *Another part of the story that Kuzey only heard about much later.*
Vex came back through the fog alone, just before dawn.

He came out of the cold gray mist at the bottom of the tower, with sand still in his hair and frost on his eyelashes, and he climbed the long stairs, round and round, slowly, to his father's map room.
His father was waiting for him. Standing at the window. With his back to the door.
"Three to one," said Mordecai Vane, without turning around.
Vex didn't say anything.
"The Keşişleme," said Mordecai. "The wind that buried fifty thousand Persians. Inside the boy. Now he has three." He was very quiet. Much too quiet. "Where is your sister?"
Vex had practiced this, the whole way through the fog. He had practiced lying. *She chased them into the desert and got lost. She's coming back tomorrow. She...*
He opened his mouth.
"She's gone," he said instead. "She went with them. She stopped me. She told me to let the girl go." He swallowed. "I couldn't freeze her, Father. I couldn't. She's my sister."
Mordecai Vane turned around.
Vex braced himself. For the shouting. For the cold. For the look on his father's face that was worse than any shouting.
But his father wasn't angry.
His father was smiling.
