"I know," said Mordecai. "I've known for weeks. Since Athens, really. I'm not a fool, Vex. Whatever else I am." He walked to the table, where the leather map was spread out. And next to the map, there was something else. A small black screen, like a phone. With a map on it. A map of the world.
And on the map, in Egypt, in Cairo, near the Nile, a tiny red dot was blinking.
*Blink. Blink. Blink.*

"Your mother's bracelet," said Mordecai softly, looking at the blinking dot. "She gave it to Vera when she was six. I put the little stone in it myself, the week after the funeral. So I would always know where my daughter was. So I would always be able to find her. Wherever she went." He touched the screen with one stone finger. "A father worries."
Vex stared at the blinking red dot.
He felt sick.

"So you see," said Mordecai, "it doesn't matter where your sister goes. Or who she goes with. She'll take me right to them. Every time." He smiled his smile, with too many teeth. "She's the most useful one of all."
He turned back to the window, where the sun was trying, and failing, to rise through the fog.
"Go and pack," he said. "Warm clothes. We're going to Japan."

Down the hall, in the cold little room at the top of the tower, Grandma Nermin sat by her window. She had heard the voices through the wall. Not the words. Just the voices. Mordecai's, cold and pleased. Vex's, small and quiet.
She closed her eyes.
Then she opened the window a crack, and whispered to the fog.

The fog didn't answer. It never did. It was Mordecai's fog, cold and dead and gray. But under the fog, very faint, there was always a little thread of real wind. A tiny breeze, slipping in from the sea. She had been talking to it every night for weeks.
"Tell him," she whispered. "Tell my Kuzey. The girl. The girl's bracelet. Tell him to look at the girl's bracelet."
The little breeze slipped out of the window and away across the gray sea.
But it was very small. And the world was very big. And it had a long, long way to go.
Vera stayed with us for three more days in Cairo, at Dr. Amira's house, while Dr. Amira's cousin found us plane tickets to Japan.
It was strange at first. For everybody.

She didn't know how to be with us. She'd been alone with her father and her brother and the Grays for so long that she'd forgotten how to be with normal people. She was very polite. Too polite. She said please and thank you for everything, even when Bora passed her the salt. She didn't laugh at jokes, or she laughed a second too late, as if she was checking first whether laughing was allowed. And she watched everything. All the time. Like someone waiting to be shouted at.
And she never, ever took off her bracelet.

On the first evening, at dinner, Bora was telling the story of the Minotaur and the baklava for the third time, with actions. When he got to the part where Asterion made the cello sound, *mmmmm,* he did the cello sound himself, very loudly, in the restaurant. And a man at the next table jumped and spilled his tea.
Vera laughed. Really laughed. Not a second too late. Right on time. A big, surprised laugh, with her head thrown back.
Then she put her hand over her mouth, as if she'd done something wrong.
"It's okay," said Ela. "You're allowed to laugh. Bora's very funny. He knows it. It's very annoying."
"I am very funny," Bora agreed.

On the second day, Dr. Amira took us all to the Citadel, an enormous old fortress on a hill above Cairo, with a huge mosque with silver domes. From the top of the walls, you could see the whole city, all the way to the pyramids.
I stood there with Vera, looking out over the city, while Uncle Tarık and Dr. Amira argued about the age of a stone.
"Can I ask you something?" said Vera.
"Sure."
"What does it feel like?" she said. "The winds. Inside you. Does it hurt?"

"No," I said. I thought about it. "It's like... having friends. Living in your chest. Three of them. They talk to each other. They argue. The North Wind is very polite, like an old teacher. The Black Wind is grumpy, like a cat. And the new one, the Keşişleme, never stops talking. It's like a man selling carpets."
Vera smiled. "That sounds nice."
"It is," I said. "Mostly. Except when they argue at three in the morning."
She was quiet for a while. She looked down at her wrist. At the bracelet.

"My father," she said, "has the Lodos in his hand. All the time. Not inside him. In his hand. And it doesn't talk to him. It screams. All the time. I can hear it, sometimes, when I stand near him. A tiny, high scream. Like a kettle." She shivered. "That's what he wants. For all of them. Seven winds, screaming."
I didn't say anything.
"I don't want that," said Vera. "I want what you have. Friends that argue at three in the morning."
At Dr. Amira's house, Ela and Vera had to share a room.

It was a small room, with two beds, a big window that looked out over the flat rooftops of Cairo, and a ceiling fan that went *whup, whup, whup* all night. Dr. Amira put them in there together on purpose. I know she did. She told Uncle Tarık, when she thought nobody was listening, "Those two girls need to talk."
They didn't talk.

Not at first. On the first night, Ela sat on her bed with the Clue Book, writing. Vera sat on her bed with her knees up, looking out of the window. Neither of them said anything. The fan went *whup, whup, whup.* Bora and I listened through the wall, and it was the most uncomfortable silence I've ever heard.
On the second night, Ela tried a test.
She wrote something on a piece of paper and passed it across to Vera without a word. Bora and I were watching through the gap in the door, which was very rude, and I'm not proud of it.

It was a code. One of Ela's codes. She makes them for fun. Letters swapped for numbers, and then the numbers shifted along by three, and then the whole thing written backwards. It took me two days to crack the last one she made. Bora has never cracked one.
Vera looked at the paper for about a minute.
Then she picked up a pencil and wrote something underneath and passed it back.
Ela read it. Her eyebrows went up. Way up.
"How did you do that so fast?" she said.

"My father used to make codes for us," said Vera. "When we were little. Before. We had to crack them to find our birthday presents." She shrugged. "That one's a Caesar shift with a number swap. Backwards. It's a good one."
Ela stared at her. Then she grabbed the paper and wrote another one, much harder, and passed it over.
Vera cracked it in four minutes.

Ela wrote another one. Vera cracked it in six. Then Vera wrote one for Ela, and Ela took eleven minutes, and was so annoyed that she threw a pillow at Vera, and Vera threw it back, and then they were both laughing.

By midnight, they were sitting on the same bed, with the Clue Book between them, making up codes together. A secret code that only the two of them would know. They wouldn't tell Bora and me how it worked, no matter how much we begged.
"It's for emergencies," said Ela. "Girl emergencies."
"What's a girl emergency?" said Bora.
"If you have to ask," said Vera, "you'll never know."
They both burst out laughing again.
Later, much later, after the lights were out, I heard them still talking through the wall. Quietly. Not about codes anymore.
"Do you miss her?" Ela asked. "Your mom?"
A long pause.
"Every day," said Vera. "Do you have a mom?"
Another long pause.

"She left," said Ela. "When I was four. She lives in Germany now, with a different family. She sends me a card on my birthday. Sometimes." The fan went *whup, whup, whup.* "So it's just me and Dad. That's why I write everything down. In the Clue Book. So I never forget anything. So nothing can just... leave."
I didn't know that. I mean, I knew Ela's mom wasn't around. But I didn't know about the Clue Book. Why she wrote everything down. I had known Ela my whole life, and I didn't know that.
"That's a good reason," said Vera softly.
"Yeah," said Ela.
The fan went *whup, whup, whup.*
"Ela?"
"Yeah?"
"What percent are you at? Trusting me?"
There was a long, long pause.
"Ninety-five," said Ela. "Don't push it."
Vera laughed, very quietly, in the dark.
"Point twenty-four," said Ela. "Three winds."

We were on Dr. Amira's roof, early in the morning, before the heat. The flat roofs of Cairo stretched away in every direction, covered in satellite dishes and water tanks and washing lines and pigeon houses. The call to prayer was echoing across the city from a thousand minarets. Far away, through the haze, you could see the tips of the pyramids.
Vera was sitting on the wall, watching. She had asked if she could come. Ela had said yes before I could even answer.
"Two was hard," I said. "Three is going to be impossible."
"Nothing is impossible," said Ela. "Some things are just very, very difficult. That's different."
"That's what my grandma says."
"I know," said Ela. "I stole it from her."
So I tried.

It was impossible. Very, very difficult, I mean. Three winds are not just one wind plus two more. They're like three different people, trying to drive the same car. The North Wind wanted to go one way, slowly and carefully. The Black Wind wanted to go another way, fast and wild. And the Keşişleme wanted to stop and chat to everyone it passed.

The first time I tried, I made a tiny snowstorm, a tiny thunderstorm and a tiny sandstorm, all at the same time, all on the roof, all crashing into each other. The result was a sort of brown, wet, icy slush that fell out of the sky onto Dr. Amira's washing.
"Point twenty-four," said Ela, wiping brown slush off her glasses, "still in progress."
The second time, the three winds had an argument inside me so loud that I fell over.
The third time, the Keşişleme told the other two a long story about a camel, and they all forgot what I'd asked them to do, and nothing happened at all.
I sat down on the roof, frustrated. "They won't work together. They're too different. They don't even *like* each other."
"Have you asked them?" said Vera quietly, from the wall.
I looked at her.
"Asked them what?"

"If they like each other," said Vera. "You said the Black Wind and the North Wind are friends now. Like brothers. Maybe the new one just needs to make friends too." She shrugged. "When I was new at school, I didn't work with anyone. I didn't know anyone. You have to know someone before you can do things together."
Ela slowly turned to look at Vera. Then at me.
"Point twenty-four B," said Ela. "Introductions."

So I sat on the roof with my eyes closed and I didn't ask the winds to do anything at all. I just let them talk. I let the North Wind tell the Keşişleme about the cistern and the carpets and the snow on Bora's eyebrows. I let the Black Wind tell it about the trolls, and the sun, and the promise. And I let the Keşişleme tell them both about the Sphinx, and the scarabs, and the soldiers singing in the desert.
It took about an hour. It was the strangest hour of my life. Like listening to three old men in a café, inside your own chest.
Then I opened my eyes.
"Okay," I said. "Can we try something together, please? All three of you? Something nice?"
The North Wind made a little cloud of snowflakes.
The Keşişleme, the desert wind, warmed them, just a little, so they turned to tiny drops of water, glittering in the morning sun.
And the Black Wind, very gently, the gentlest I'd ever felt it, spun the drops around in the sunlight.
And there, above the rooftop, above the satellite dishes and the washing lines, in the hot morning air of Cairo, was a rainbow.
A small one. A perfect one. A complete circle of color, red and orange and yellow and green and blue and purple, hanging in the air above our heads, sparkling.
Vera's mouth fell open.
Ela lowered the Clue Book very, very slowly.
On the next roof, an old woman hanging up her washing dropped a whole basket of sheets and said something in Arabic that made Dr. Amira, downstairs, laugh out loud.
"Point twenty-four," said Ela softly. "Complete."
The rainbow hung there for a long time. Then, slowly, it faded, and the little drops of water fell on our faces like warm rain.
*That,* said the Keşişleme, deeply impressed, *was beautiful. I have never made a beautiful thing before. Only big ones.*
*Beautiful is better,* said the North Wind.
*Hmph,* said the Black Wind. Which, for the Black Wind, is a compliment.
That night, I couldn't sleep. Again.
The Keşişleme wouldn't stop talking.

It was the newest wind inside me, and it was so different from the others. The North Wind was quiet and polite. The Black Wind was moody and silent most of the time. But the Keşişleme talked and talked and talked. About camels it had known. About caravans it had chased. About cities it had covered in sand, and kings it had blown the crowns off, and a Roman general whose toga it had once blown completely over his head in front of his whole army.
It was very funny. And very annoying at three in the morning.
"Please," I whispered, lying in the dark. "Can you be quiet for a bit? I need to sleep."
*Sleep! Ha! Sleep is for camels!* said the Keşişleme. *Let me tell you about the time I...*
"The Persian army," I said.
The Keşişleme stopped.
"The Sphinx said you buried an army. Fifty thousand men. In one afternoon." I stared at the ceiling. "Is that true?"
For a long time, the desert wind said nothing at all. It was the first time it had been silent since it came inside me.
*Yes,* it said at last. Quietly.
And then it showed me.

I don't know how. One moment I was lying on Dr. Amira's sofa in the dark. The next moment I was in the desert. Not really. But it felt real. A huge, empty desert, golden and burning, under a white sky. And marching across it, a long, long line of soldiers. Thousands and thousands of them. With spears and shields and helmets, and camels and horses and wagons, stretching all the way to the horizon. Their armor flashed in the sun.

They were tired. You could see it. Their feet were dragging. Their faces were burned by the sun. They had been walking for days. Some of them were singing, to keep going. A sad song, in a language I didn't know.

*Their king sent them,* said the Keşişleme softly. *Cambyses. A cruel king. He sent them to attack a temple in the desert, a temple of the god Amun, because the priests had said something he did not like. He did not care about the soldiers. He did not care if they lived or died. He only wanted to win.*
In front of the army, on the horizon, a wall was rising. A wall of brown and gold. Rolling across the desert. Getting bigger. Getting closer.
A sandstorm.
*And the priests of Amun called me,* said the Keşişleme. *They knew how. They were the Order, then, before it had a name. They called me and they said, protect the temple. And I came.*
The soldiers saw the wall coming. They stopped singing. They started to run. But there was nowhere to run. The desert was flat and empty in every direction.
I closed my eyes. I didn't want to see it. But I could still hear it. The roar. The wind.
When I opened them, I was back on the sofa, in the dark. My face was wet.

*I protected the temple,* said the Keşişleme, very quietly. *That is what they asked. But those men were not bad men. They were tired, and hungry, and far from home. They had mothers. They were singing.* It paused. *I have thought about their song for two and a half thousand years.*
I lay there for a long time.
"Is that why you laugh so much?" I asked. "And talk all the time? So you don't have to think about it?"
The Keşişleme didn't answer for a long time.
*You are very clever for a small boy,* it said finally. *Too clever. It is annoying.*
"Ela says that too."

*The girl with the book is right.* A pause. *The cold man wants me because I can do that. Bury armies. He would send me against cities. Against people. Again and again. And I would have to.* Another pause. *You said no. In the tomb. When I offered. You said no.*
"I'll always say no," I said.
*I know,* said the Keşişleme. *That is why I came to you.*
It was quiet after that. All three winds were quiet. And I fell asleep at last, and dreamed about a long line of soldiers, singing, walking home.
On our last afternoon in Cairo, Bora made us go back to the pyramids.
"I have to say goodbye," he said. "To Mustafa. I promised."
"You promised a *camel?*" said Ela.
"I promised a *friend,*" said Bora, with great dignity.
So we went. All of us. Even Vera, who had never met a camel and was a little bit afraid of them, after the stories Bora had told about how much they spit.

Mustafa was standing in the same place, by the road below the Sphinx, with his colorful blanket and his tassels, looking bored and annoyed, as usual. His owner, the young man with the big smile, was shouting "Camel ride! Very good price!" at a group of tourists.
When Mustafa saw Bora, he did something nobody expected.

He made a noise. A loud, long, happy, gurgling noise, like a drain unblocking. And he walked straight over to Bora, pulling his owner along behind him on the rope, and pushed his big hairy head into Bora's chest so hard that Bora fell over backwards into the sand.
"He's happy to see you," said Vera, astonished.

"He says," said Bora, from the sand, laughing, "where have you *been?* He says the tourists today are terrible. One of them tried to ride him while eating an ice cream. He says the ice cream fell on his ear."
The owner was staring at Bora with his mouth open. "My camel," he said, in English. "My camel never does this. Never. He hates everybody. He even hates me, a little."
"He doesn't hate you," said Bora, getting up. "He says you sing badly. But he likes you. He says you give him the good dates. The soft ones."
The young man's face went through about five different expressions. Then he laughed, and shook his head, and laughed again.
"How do you know that?" he said. "About the dates? Nobody knows that."
Bora just shrugged and smiled.

He had brought a whole bag of carrots. He'd bought them that morning at the market. He gave them to Mustafa one by one, very slowly, and Mustafa ate each one with great dignity, chewing with his big lower lip, making little happy grumbling noises.
The rest of us stood a little way away and waited.

When the last carrot was gone, Bora put his hand on Mustafa's neck, and stood very close to him, and talked for a long time. Very quietly. None of us could hear what he said. Mustafa listened, with his long eyelashes half closed, his ears turning to Bora's voice.
Then the camel bent his long neck down, and rested his chin on top of Bora's head for a moment. Very gently. Like a hug.
When Bora came back to us, his eyes were wet.
"What did he say?" asked Ela softly.

Bora wiped his nose. "He said," he said, "that in twenty years of carrying tourists, nobody ever asked him what he thought about anything. He said I was the first." He sniffed. "And he said, if I ever come back, he'll give me a free ride. And he won't spit on me. Not even once."
"That's very generous," said Uncle Tarık seriously. "For a camel."
"It's the most generous thing a camel has ever said," said Bora.
As we drove away in Dr. Amira's little car, back toward the city, I looked back.
Mustafa was standing by the road below the Sphinx, watching us go. His owner was standing next to him, scratching his head, still looking confused.
And behind them both, the great stone lion lay on the sand with its paws stretched out, looking at the sunrise, calm and patient, the way it had for five thousand years.
I thought I saw it wink. But that was probably just the light.

chapters.t: Chapter Thirty-Three: The Felucca at Night
p: On our last night in Cairo, Abu Hassan took us sailing again. All of us. Including Vera.

We went out after dark, when the city lights were reflected in the river in long, wobbly lines of gold and red and green. The felucca slid out onto the black water, its big white sail glowing in the lights from the bridges. The honking of the city faded behind us. There was only the soft lap of the water against the boat, and Abu Hassan humming an old song.
This time, I didn't need to ask the wind. The Nile wind came by itself, gentle and warm, and filled the sail.
*For the Windborn,* it said, sleepily. *And his friends.*

Bora lay on his back, eating sugar cane, which he had discovered that week and now ate constantly. Ela sat next to Uncle Tarık, reading him bits of the Clue Book out loud. Dr. Amira was arguing with her uncle about something in Arabic, and both of them were laughing.
Vera sat at the very front of the boat, alone, looking at the water.
I went and sat next to her.
For a while, neither of us said anything. The lights of Cairo slid by. A fish jumped somewhere in the dark, with a little splash.

"My mother loved boats," Vera said at last. "She grew up by the sea. In Cornwall, in England. Her father was a fisherman." She trailed her fingers in the water. "She used to take us out in a little rowing boat, when we were small. Me and Vex. Every summer. She'd row us out to where the seals were, and we'd sit very still and watch them. And she'd tell us their names. She gave every seal a name."
"What happened to her?" I asked. Then I wished I hadn't. "Sorry. You don't have to..."

"She got sick," said Vera simply. "When we were six. Very fast. Three months, and she was gone." She looked at the bracelet on her wrist. "She gave me this, two weeks before. She said, 'To keep you safe. Wherever you go.' And she gave Vex a little silver compass. He lost it, years ago. He cried for a week. He doesn't remember that, I think. Or he says he doesn't."
The felucca turned slowly in the wind. The sail flapped, then filled again.

"My father changed after that," said Vera. "Everyone says it was the gray hand that changed him. The old book. But I think it started before. When she died. I think he was so sad that he wanted to never feel anything again. And the gray hand helped." She swallowed. "Grandma Nermin says that too. She said it to him once. I heard her through the door. She said, 'Mordecai, you're not cold. You're sad. They're not the same thing.'"
"What did he say?"
"He left the room," said Vera. "He slammed the door. He never slams doors."
The wind sighed around the sail.
"Do you think," I said slowly, "that he could change back?"
Vera was quiet for a very long time.
"I don't know," she said. "I used to think so. When I was little. Now I don't know." She looked at me. "Do *you* think so?"
I thought about the face in the northern lights. *It feels like being outside a house, in the cold, looking through the window at a family having dinner. Forever.*
"I think he's very lonely," I said. "And I think that's a thing that can change. Maybe."
Vera looked out at the dark river for a long time.
Then, very quietly, she said, "Thank you."

At the back of the boat, Abu Hassan started to sing. An old song, in Arabic, slow and sad and beautiful. Dr. Amira joined in. Then, after a moment, Uncle Tarık started humming along, even though he didn't know the words, and Bora started drumming on the side of the boat with his sugar cane.
And Vera Vane, the daughter of the Gray Hand, sitting at the front of a little boat on the Nile, in the dark, with the lights of the city all around her, started to laugh.
When we came back from the river that night, Dr. Amira was waiting for us at her house with an envelope.

"My cousin," she said, "works for an airline. A very small airline. Not a very good one. But it flies to Tokyo." She opened the envelope and spread out five tickets on the bed. "The seats are next to the toilets. I'm sorry. It was all he could do."
"We're used to it," said Bora. "We're toilet-seat professionals."
"Five tickets," said Ela, counting. "Dad, me, Kuzey, Bora... and Vera."
Vera stared at the tickets.
"For me?" she said.
"Of course for you," said Dr. Amira. "You're one of the team now. Aren't you?"
Vera looked at all of us. Then she nodded. Very fast, and looked away, and rubbed her eyes with the back of her hand, the hand with the bracelet on it.
Later, I spread the leather map of the Seven Winds on the bed for the last time in Egypt.
Four stars were dark now. Istanbul. Crete. Iceland. Egypt.
And far to the east, across the whole width of Asia, past deserts and mountains and oceans, a new star was glowing. Red and gold, like the sunrise.
"Japan," said Uncle Tarık. He looked a bit pale. "I really don't have that many airline miles left. I used the last of them in Iceland."
"Don't worry," said Dr. Amira. "I paid for these. With my own money." She smiled. "Bring me back a story, Tarık. A good one. And a postcard. And bring yourself back in one piece."
She hugged him. And then she hugged each of us. When she hugged me, she whispered in my ear.

"Your grandmother," she whispered, "came into my office forty years ago and changed my life. You know that? I became an Egyptologist because of her. Because of the tablet. Because I wanted to know what it meant." She held me at arm's length and looked at me with her bright, sharp eyes. "Now I know. Bring her home, Kuzey. I want to thank her."
I lay awake for a long time that night, listening to the three winds inside me whispering together in the dark.
The North Wind was talking about snow. The Black Wind was talking about clouds. The Keşişleme was telling them both a story about a caravan of a thousand camels it had once chased across the Sahara.
Somewhere out there, my grandmother was in a gray tower by the sea. Singing.
Somewhere out there, Vex was alone with a father who was turning him to stone.
And somewhere out there, Mordecai Vane was packing his bags. Going to Japan in person.
For the first time, it wouldn't be the twins we were racing.
It would be him.
In the next room, I could hear Vera breathing, slow and steady, asleep. And on her wrist, so quiet that nobody could hear it, the little gray stone in her mother's bracelet went on clicking.
*Click. Click. Click.*

For hundreds of years, sailors on the Black Sea, the Bosphorus and the Mediterranean used a wind rose to name the winds. Each wind had its own name and its own personality, and every sailor knew them by heart. These are the seven winds of the Order of the Compass Rose.
**Yıldız (North).** Named after the North Star, *yıldız* means "star." A cold, clear, starry wind. Kuzey's own wind.
**Poyraz (Northeast).** The great wind of the Black Sea. When the Poyraz blows hard, the fishermen go home and the ferries rock.
**Gündoğusu (East).** "Sunrise." The wind that comes from where the sun is born each morning.
**Keşişleme (Southeast).** Named after the monks, the *keşiş,* who lived on the mountains to the southeast. A warm, dry wind from the deserts.
**Kıble (South).** The wind from the direction of Mecca. Hot, and full of sand.
**Lodos (Southwest).** A warm, wild, wet wind that brings big waves and headaches. People in Istanbul say the Lodos makes everyone grumpy.
**Karayel (Northwest).** "Black wind." A stormy, dark wind that brings clouds and sudden rain.
And the eighth, the west wind, the **Batı**, the one that would not make a deal? Nobody knows. It is still wild. That is another story.

chapters.t: The Real Places in This Book
p: **Khan el-Khalili.** The great old bazaar of Cairo, full of brass lamps, spices, perfume bottles and shopkeepers who will tell you that just looking is free.
**The Egyptian Museum.** A huge pink building in Cairo, full of statues, coffins, mummies and treasures from five thousand years of Egyptian history. Cats really do live around it.
**Shu.** The ancient Egyptian god of air and wind, who held up the sky goddess Nut, so that there would be space between the sky and the earth.
**Bronze mirrors.** The ancient Egyptians really did use polished metal mirrors. Some historians think they used mirrors to reflect sunlight into tombs, so painters could see.
**Feluccas.** Small wooden sailboats with one big triangular sail. They've sailed on the Nile for thousands of years, and still do.

**The Great Pyramid.** Built about 4,500 years ago, from more than two million stone blocks. For almost 4,000 years, it was the tallest building on Earth. You can climb up inside it, through the Grand Gallery, to the King's Chamber, where there's an empty stone box. Air shafts really do point north and south.
**The workers' village.** Archaeologists really did find the town where the pyramid builders lived, with bakeries. They ate bread, onions, fish and meat.

**The Sphinx.** Carved out of the bedrock itself, about 73 meters long, with the head of a pharaoh. Its nose is missing. At sunset on the equinoxes, the sun sets very close to the right shoulder of the Sphinx, as seen from in front of it. Everyone knows the Greek riddle. Nobody has ever been asked a second one. As far as we know.
**The lost army of Cambyses.** An old story from the Greek historian Herodotus says a Persian army of fifty thousand men was buried by a sandstorm in the western desert. Nobody has ever found it.
**Koshari.** Rice, lentils, macaroni, chickpeas, crispy onions and tomato sauce. Really delicious.
*Here is the first chapter of the next book,* The Thunder Drum.
**Chapter One: Toilet Seats to Tokyo**
The flight from Cairo to Tokyo takes fourteen hours. We sat next to the toilets for every one of them.
"Toilet-seat professionals," said Bora, settling in with a bag of Egyptian sweets and a neck pillow shaped like a crocodile. "This is our natural home."

Every few minutes, the toilet door banged open and shut, and somebody squeezed past our knees. The toilet flushed with a sound like a jet engine. The smell drifted over us in little clouds. Ela put on a sleep mask and earplugs and pretended she was somewhere else. Uncle Tarık fell asleep in about four minutes and slept for nine hours, snoring, with his mouth open and a book called *Myths and Legends of Old Japan* on his chest.
Vera sat by the window. She had never been on a normal plane before.
"Never?" said Bora, amazed. "Not even once?"

"We always went through the fog," said Vera. She was pressed against the window, watching the desert slide away underneath us, gold and brown and endless. "My father doesn't like planes. Too many people. Too slow." She smiled a little. "I like it. You can see everything."

She watched out of the window for hours. The desert. Then the sea, blue and wrinkled. Then mountains, brown and huge. Then clouds. Then, as it got dark, the lights of cities, scattered across the ground like spilled glitter.
I watched her watching. I thought about what she'd said, in Egypt. *I want what you have. Friends that argue at three in the morning.*
She kept touching her bracelet. The silver one, with the little gray stone. Turning it around and around her wrist, without seeming to notice.
Somewhere over India, I fell asleep.

I dreamed of the wind. Not my three winds. A different one. A soft, warm, golden wind, coming from far in the east, from where the sun rises. It blew across a sea of clouds, and over a mountain covered in snow. And on the mountain, something was waiting for me. Something very big, and very old, with a bag on its back.
And something else was coming toward the mountain too. From the north. Through the fog.
Something cold.
I woke up with a jolt. The plane was dark and humming. Everyone was asleep. Even Vera, with her head against the window.
Except, at the window, the little gray stone in her bracelet was glinting in the light from the toilet sign.
*Click. Click. Click.*
I didn't hear it. Not then. Nobody could have heard it.
But somewhere very far away, on a small black screen in a gray tower, a red dot was moving east.
§END To be continued in* The Thunder Drum...
